newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Visitors use flashlights to see Marcos corpse.
newsitem.headline: Visitors use flashlights to see Marcos corpse.

text.p: Visitors used flashlights on Tuesday to peer at the corpse of Ferdinand Marcos after a Philippine power firm, saddled with unpaid bills, shut down electricity in his mausoleum.

Tomb caretakers wept, while the former president's widow Imelda called the decision to turn off the power macabre and repeated her family would not pay the bills amounting to 5.643 million pesos ($214,500).

Jesus Nalupta, mayor of Marcos's hometown of Batac, said he would try to help by paying part of the bills out of his own pocket and by charging tourists entrance fees if they wanted to see the preserved cadaver.
A sign hanging outside the mausoleum read: "BROWNOUT".
A family source said the Marcoses planned to buy a generator to get power running again pending negotiations on how to settle the bills.
Marcos died in exile in Hawaii in 1989 three years after he was ousted in a popular revolt that ended his 20-year rule.
President Fidel Ramos, who is now visiting India, allowed the remains to be brought to Batac in Ilocos Norte province but refused to allow it to be buried in Manila, fearing unrest.
The corpse, injected with chemicals that embalmers said would preserve it for 10 years, has since lain in an elevated glass coffin in the air-conditioned mausoleum in the family backyard.
Up until Monday, the corpse had been bathed in soft lights 24 hours a day while classical music played in the background.
A group of journalists and a few curious visitors stepped into the eerie darkness of the mausoleum on Tuesday and, turning on their flashlights, peered into Marcos's face.
A day after the power was shut off, the glass coffin appeared already to be gathering moisture.
"It's shocking," Imelda Marcos, now a congresswoman, told Reuters in Manila. "Is this the policy of government? It is so macabre... This is not done to human beings, least of all to the dead."

Marcos said she could not pay the bills because the state had seized all of the family's property. The government has accused the Marcoses of stealing up to $5 billion from the economy during their rule and has sequestered their assets pending a court ruling on their ownership.
Imelda Marcos was convicted of corruption in 1993 and sentenced to 18 years in prison. She is appealing the case and is out on bail.
"I am left with nothing because we've been deprived of everything," she said.

Joel Jose, who works as a mausoleum cleaner, cried when the electric cooperative disconnected the power line. "I was crying because I pity Apo (Sir)," Jose said. "It's only electricity and even that they won't give to him."
